newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom enters hot phase of listing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche Telekom enters hot phase of listing.

text.p: German telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom (DT) on Friday began the hot phase of what is expected to be Europe's largest-ever share listing, by promising investors generous dividends and strong growth.

DT chief finance officer Joachim Kroeske presented the company's preliminary sales prospectus ahead of its listing next month, which could raise between 13-17 billion marks ($8.5-$11.1 billion), depending on the price and number of shares.
Trading in DT shares on stock exchanges in Germany and New York will begin on November 18 and start a day later in Tokyo.

The issue will dwarf Germany's previously largest offering, the privatisation of Veba AG, and could spark a move by traditionally conservative German private investors towards greater purchase of stocks.
"We have done everything we could for private investors within the realm of possibility for an investment in stocks," Kroeske told a news conference at DT's head offices in Bonn.
Unlike British Telecom (BT), which was sold to the public more than 10 years ago, Deutsche Telekom will immediately be set out in a harsh competitive environment.
Competition, already burning away some of the company's business, will turn red-hot in 1998 when the telecommunications sector throughout Europe is deregulated.

At home DT's main competitors will be the DBKom group consisting of Mannesmann AG, the German railway, the European Unisource alliance and AT&T Corp, a consortium between British Telecom and utilities RWE AG and Viag AG, and the alliance between Veba AG and Cable and Wireless.

"Deutsche Telekom will lose more market share by the year 2003, five years after the end of its monopoly, than BT lost from 1990 to 1995," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, the investment arm of Deutsche Bank, a manager of the DT listing.

But the bank added that DT's competitors will probably achieve total turnover in 2005 of just 11 billion marks, well below their expectations. The German telecommunications market is expected to be worth over 100 billion marks by 2000.

Addressing weaknesses in the company's balance sheet, Kroeske said DT would cut its huge mountain of debt to 65 billion marks by the year 2000 from 107 billion marks. The company also plans to cut its workforce to 170,000 employees in 2000, from 230,000 when it was incorporated in 1995.

Faced with a hard sell, DT has spent just under 100 million marks in advertising the shares and is offering incentives to private investors. Based on an offer of 500 million new shares, it plans to pay a dividend of 60 pfennigs a share for 1996.
Shares are eligible for dividends for the full year, although investors will only hold shares for six weeks of the year. DT plans to pay a dividend of around 1.20 marks for 1997.

Kroeske declined to comment on how dividends would be affected if the banks take up the 75 million additional shares in the so-called "greenshoe" offering in the event that demand is greater than expected.

Private German investors who register with the company by October 11 will receive preferential treatment in the allocation of shares and those who hold their shares for three years will then receive one bonus share for every ten held.

German investors must buy a minimum of 100 shares and the special conditions apply to an investment of up to 300 shares a person. More than two million Germans have registered with the company. Half of those have never owned shares before.

Non-German investors will not be subject to German taxes, unless the depositary bank held shares in Germany for some time. But non-German shareholders will not be eligible for a refundable tax credit that German shareholders receive.

DT will set the price of the shares during the weekend ahead of its November 18 listing. The share price will be determined in a bookbuilding procedure that begins on October 22, when bids are take from institutional investors.

Shares are expected to cost between 20 marks and 30 marks, slightly lower than DT's own expectations. If a compromise of 25 marks is reached on the share price, then the DT public offering would generate just 12.5 billion marks for 500 million, less than the target of 15 billion marks. ($1=1.5306 Mark)
